rv.q: Atri Banerjee’s production of the Shakespeare summer favourite is winningly vivid
Crucially, it lacks enchantment. A mixed bag.
Yet even with Maimuna Memon’s escapist, trippy folk score, the overall effect is confused and ponderous.
It’s just a bit disjointed, and less of a laugh than it should be.
A Midsummer Night's Dream is a must-see show this summer for anybody wanting to immerse themselves in a spellbinding and twisting tale filled with raucous laughter.

What we witnessed was an enchanting production that was experimental with the inclusion of a live folk band on stage, creating a festival-style fairy realm with a huge nod to the Pagan origins in the text.

Though a bit of a tricky abstract start (a blank canvas on which to sketch, a drama school analysis), I can see where director Atri Banerjee is heading with his minimalist, stripped to bare bones version.

There's much to applaud in this exuberant and entertaining A Midsummer Night's Dream, even though at times speech was a bit muddied and the production could be tightened so the audience gets home before Fairy Hour.

Fortunately, if the set disappoints, the cast is fully equipped to bring out the humour. Oliver Huband (fresh from A Doll’s House at the Almeida) is a commanding presence as Theseus and a screwball as Oberon. Though the question remains: Why does he want Titania’s Indian changeling so much?

The production is on the languid side, and this isn’t the funniest, most coherent or most visually beautiful Dream ever (the concurrent production at the Globe sounds more successful in creating a sense of unified elation).

But perhaps in an attempt to attract a less likely audience, Banerjee has drowned all of this in a wash of wholesomeness and uncomplicated joy, which might sound nice but makes for a boring production.
It is an inventive, inclusive and hugely entertaining production that reminds us why Shakespeare's most magical comedy continues to cast its spell.
It is ideal as a setting for Shakespeare’s Dream, especially a production as successful as Banerjee’s.
This A Midsummer Night’s Dream is an enjoyable if uneven affair.
Whilst some choices feel somewhat clunky within the motion of the play, others are revelations that invigorate the work.
This production tends to sit more in the middle ground; entertaining but neither rip-roaringly hilarious nor challenging in its handling of difficult issues.
Atri Banerjee's 2026 punt gives the play a folk-rock aesthetic, complete with a punkish fairy band and neon dip dyed hair Titania, but ultimately struggles to take flight.
This has been my favourite thing to watch in a long time: a night where everything lines up to create something genuinely special.
By the second half, whether through a second glass of wine or the accumulating magic of the evening, the wooden steps had become an enchanted forest, and I was entirely under its spell.

By trusting Shakespeare's original work rather than trying to transform it into something entirely different, Student Group 78 has produced a version that feels authentic, engaging and refreshingly confident.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this meta, countercultural production at Regent's Park. While some praise its humor and the magical outdoor setting, many criticize the stark wooden design that clashes with the natural surroundings.
